content: The severity of anemia is classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on hemoglobin concentrations. These are defined as greater than 80%, between 80% and 60%, or less than 60% of the cutoff levels, respectively. However, a review and recalculation of the World Health Organization (WHO) anemia severity cutoffs revealed broader ranges: 85–92% of the cutoff value for mild anemia and 62–70% for severe anemia. Consequently, the cutoff for severe anemia in children aged 6–23 months and women in their second trimester of pregnancy was retained at less than 70 g/L. For example, a hemoglobin level of 80 g/L in girls aged 12–17 years represents 67% of the cutoff of 120 g/L. Similarly, a hemoglobin level of 70 g/L in pregnant women during the second trimester corresponds to 67% of the cutoff of 105 g/L, aligning with the use of 70 g/L for pregnant women in the first and third trimesters, which is 64% of the cutoff of 110 g/L. For mild anemia, 95 g/L represents 90% of the cutoff of 105 g/L. The hemoglobin cutoffs for defining anemia severity in various populations are as follows: Children aged 6–23 months: No anemia (≥105 g/L), mild anemia (95–104 g/L), moderate anemia (70–94 g/L), severe anemia (<70 g/L). Children aged 24–59 months: No anemia (≥110 g/L), mild anemia (100–109 g/L), moderate anemia (70–99 g/L), severe anemia (<70 g/L). Children aged 5–11 years: No anemia (≥115 g/L), mild anemia (110–114 g/L), moderate anemia (80–109 g/L), severe anemia (<80 g/L). Children aged 12–14 years (non-pregnant girls and boys): No anemia (≥120 g/L), mild anemia (110–119 g/L), moderate anemia (80–109 g/L), severe anemia (<80 g/L). Non-pregnant women aged 15–65 years: No anemia (≥120 g/L), mild anemia (110–119 g/L), moderate anemia (80–109 g/L), severe anemia (<80 g/L). Men aged 15–65 years: No anemia (≥130 g/L), mild anemia (110–129 g/L), moderate anemia (80–109 g/L), severe anemia (<80 g/L). Pregnancy (first trimester ≥110 g/L, second trimester ≥105 g/L, third trimester ≥110 g/L): Mild anemia (95–104 g/L in the second trimester, 100–109 g/L in the first and third trimesters), moderate anemia (70–94 g/L in the second trimester, 70–99 g/L in the first and third trimesters), severe anemia (<70 g/L in all trimesters). The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based hemoglobin cutoffs to define anemia and its severity. These cutoffs were informed by analyses of international databases containing hemoglobin and other biochemical and clinical indicators from healthy, ethnically diverse populations, primarily from high-income settings. Additional data from lower-income settings showed variability but generally lower hemoglobin values among participants without evidence of iron or vitamin A deficiencies or inflammation. However, these data were excluded from pooled analyses due to the potential residual effects of infections and inflammation on hemoglobin concentrations. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) retained the hemoglobin cutoff of 130 g/L for men after considering concerns about the implications of iron therapy, limited evidence, and potential unintended consequences of changing the cutoff. The GDG prioritized avoiding harm and ensuring accurate anemia diagnoses at both clinical and public health levels. Adjustments to hemoglobin concentrations for external factors such as elevation of residence and smoking are recommended to improve the accuracy of anemia diagnosis. For elevation, hemoglobin adjustments are based on increments of 500 meters above sea level, with specific values subtracted from observed hemoglobin levels or added to anemia cutoffs. For example, at elevations of 500–999 meters, 4 g/L is subtracted, while at 2000–2499 meters, 14 g/L is subtracted. Adjustments for very high elevations (>3000 meters) are primarily based on data from Central and South America, and tailored adjustments by region or ethnicity may be warranted. For smoking, hemoglobin adjustments are based on the number of cigarettes smoked per day. For example, 3 g/L is added for smokers with unknown quantity or those smoking fewer than 10 cigarettes per day, 5 g/L for 10–19 cigarettes per day, and 6 g/L for more than 20 cigarettes per day. The GDG determined that hemoglobin concentrations should not be adjusted for infection and inflammation due to the complexity and variability of their effects on hemoglobin levels. Instead, additional indicators are needed to establish the underlying causes and magnitude of anemia in such cases. In summary, the GDG emphasized the importance of accurate hemoglobin cutoffs and adjustments to define anemia and its severity, considering factors such as elevation and smoking. These adjustments are critical for understanding anemia prevalence, implementing effective health interventions, and improving the health and nutrition status of individuals and populations.
